categories.name: Basics & politeness
categories.blurb: The 20 phrases that carry the whole trip.
tips: Sumimasen is your Swiss-army word: excuse me, sorry, and thank you for the trouble.
A small nod or bow with arigatō goes a long way. You don't need a deep bow.
Add -san after other people's names, never your own.
The u in desu and masu is barely said: "dess", "mass".

categories.name: How to pronounce
categories.blurb: Five rules that make romaji sound right.
tips: Vowels are always the same: a = ah, i = ee, u = oo, e = eh, o = oh.
A line over a vowel (ō, ū) means hold it twice as long. It changes the word.
Double consonants (kk, tt, pp, ss) get a tiny pause: kitte = kit-te.
R is a light tap, halfway between r, l and d.
Keep every syllable even. Japanese has no strong stress like English.

categories.name: Restaurants
categories.blurb: Getting seated, ordering, diet needs and paying.
tips: No tipping, ever. Leaving cash can cause staff to chase you down to return it.
Say sumimasen! with a raised hand to call staff. Many tables have a call button instead.
Pay at the register by the door, not at the table. Bring the check slip with you.
Say gochisōsama deshita on the way out. Staff love hearing it.
Ramen and gyūdon shops often use a ticket machine at the entrance. Buy first, hand the ticket over.

categories.name: Bars & izakaya
categories.blurb: Drinks, kanpai, cover charges and last call.
tips: Many izakaya add a small cover charge with a snack you didn't order (otōshi). It's normal, not a scam.
Wait until everyone has a drink, then kanpai together before sipping.
Pour for others, not yourself. Someone will refill your glass in return.
Nomihōdai is all-you-can-drink for a set time, usually 90 to 120 minutes.

categories.name: Trains, taxis & buses
categories.blurb: IC cards, platforms, shinkansen and taxis.
tips: Keep calls off and voices low on trains. Set your phone to silent mode.
Queue at the floor markings on the platform and let people off first.
Tokyo stands on the LEFT of escalators. Osaka stands on the RIGHT. Kyoto is mixed.
Taxi doors open and close by themselves. Don't touch the rear door.

An IC card (Suica, PASMO or ICOCA, as a card or in Apple Wallet) works on almost all trains, buses and konbini. Suica in Google Wallet only works on Android phones bought in Japan, so with a US phone buy a physical card at a station ticket machine and top it up with cash.

categories.name: Hotel & ryokan
categories.blurb: Check-in, luggage, Wi-Fi and ryokan life.
tips: Shoes off at the ryokan entrance and wherever the floor steps up. Never step on tatami in slippers.
Wear the yukata left side over right. Right over left is how the dead are dressed.
Ryokan dinner is usually at a set time. Tell them if you'll be late.
Most hotels hold luggage before check-in and after check-out for free.

categories.name: Shopping & konbini
categories.blurb: Konbini questions, sizes, tax-free and paying.
tips: Put cash or your card in the little tray by the register, not in the cashier's hand.
Bags cost a few yen. The cashier will ask if you want one.

Tax-free needs your physical passport. Until October 31, 2026 the tax comes off at the register. From November 1, 2026 you pay full price, scan your passport at the airport before check-in, and the store refunds the tax afterwards.
Haggling isn't done, except maybe at flea markets.

categories.name: Sightseeing & tickets
categories.blurb: Tickets, photos, lockers and opening hours.
tips: Look for "no photo" signs (撮影禁止) inside temples and museums.
Coin lockers at stations are the easiest way to drop bags for the day. Many take IC cards.
Popular spots like teamLab or the Ghibli Museum sell out. Book ahead online.

categories.name: Directions
categories.blurb: Asking the way, left, right, and near or far.
tips: Point at a map on your phone and say: koko ni ikitai desu (I want to go here).
Police boxes (kōban) are everywhere and officers happily give directions.
Station staff and konbini clerks are also good people to ask.

categories.name: Numbers, money & time
categories.blurb: Prices, times, how many and how long.
tips: Japanese counts in 10,000s (man). ¥10,000 = ichi-man en. ¥30,000 = san-man en.
Ordering by count: hitotsu (1), futatsu (2), mittsu (3) works for almost any item.
Holding up fingers works fine when ordering. Nobody will mind.

categories.name: Emergencies & health
categories.blurb: Help, police, pharmacy, doctor and lost items.
tips: Dial 119 for ambulance or fire. Dial 110 for police.
Japan Visitor Hotline (24 h, English): 050-3816-2787.
Lost items are very often turned in. Ask at the station office or the nearest kōban.
Drugstores (doraggusutoa) sell basics. Prescription medicine comes from a pharmacy (yakkyoku).

categories.name: Onsen, shrines & temples
categories.blurb: Bathing rules, tattoos, shrine and temple manners.
tips: Wash and rinse fully at the shower stools BEFORE getting in the bath.
No swimsuits. The small towel never goes in the water. Rest it on your head or the edge.
Many onsen ban tattoos. Ask first, or use a private bath (kashikiri).
At a shrine: bow twice, clap twice, pray, bow once. At a temple: no clapping.
Walk along the sides of the shrine path. The center is for the gods.

categories.name: Small talk
tips: People may ask where you're from and if you like Japanese food. Short answers are perfect.
Japanese people often downplay compliments. Keep yours simple and sincere.
